headline: Mozambique Officially Protects Mount Mabu, Home to Butterfly Paradise
meta_description: Mozambique has formally protected Mount Mabu, a biodiversity hotspot with over 200 butterfly species, granting stewardship to local communities.
summary_short: Mozambique has officially protected Mount Mabu, a forest in northern Mozambique that hosts over 200 butterfly species and dozens of newly discovered animals.
body:
In a major conservation victory, Mozambique has formally protected Mount Mabu, a 9,341-hectare forest reserve in the Lugela district of northern Mozambique that has earned the nickname "butterfly forest" for its extraordinary abundance of winged life. The Ministry of Agriculture, Environment and Fisheries published the decree on August 24, establishing the Mount Mabu Community Conservation Area with a crucial twist: stewardship of the land has been granted to the local communities who have safeguarded the forest for generations. Scientists have documented more than 200 butterfly species at Mount Mabu, with researchers estimating the true number could reach 250 as surveys continue. The protection represents recognition that community custodianship, not fortress conservation, has proven most effective here.

The forest's magic lies in its geography. Mount Mabu's steep ridges and valleys, rising to 1,700 meters, create isolated microclimates where species evolved in near-total isolation over millions of years. Since 2005, scientists have discovered more than 30 previously unknown species within its boundaries—from frogs and chameleons to a cobalt-blue butterfly, Iolaus mabuensis, of which only a single specimen has ever been collected. Each October and November, hundreds of butterflies gather on the summit in a mating behavior called hilltopping, a phenomenon so striking that naturalist David Attenborough documented it on film.

Ecologist Julian Bayliss, whose 20 years of surveys helped build the case for protection, calls Mount Mabu's high levels of endemism—species found nowhere else—crucial to preserve. While small-scale agriculture and logging remain threats, the forest's sacred status among locals has kept it largely intact. The decree dedicates Mount Mabu to conservation and sustainable use by the communities who protected it when few others recognized its value.
quick_facts: 9,341 hectares of forest formally protected in northern Mozambique
Over 200 butterfly species documented; potentially 250 with further surveys
30+ new animal species discovered since 2005, including a cobalt-blue butterfly
Stewardship granted to local communities, not government agencies
Hundreds of butterflies gather for mating season each October and November
